Hinged Pythagoras 2

GeometryAreaTriangles
Game: This is a picture to explore, not a game to win: four triangles swing on two hinges inside a square.
How to play: Drag the gold points or use the two sliders to change the swing and the triangle shape. Press Turn to the end or Reset.

Look for the math

The applet shows a droodle — "What is it?" — with two copies of one square. On the left, four triangles are cut loose from a small square in the middle; on the right, two of those triangles swing about the orange hinges. The shape changes, but the pieces do not.

Four triangles and a small square

The "Triangle shape" slider sets an angle B. The cut-out is a right triangle with legs a = c·cos B, b = c·sin B and sloping side c, the side of the square. Each of the four congruent triangles has area ab/2, and the small square in the middle has side |a−b|.

Why the turn cannot change the area

Swinging a triangle about a hinge is a rigid turn: its side lengths and its area stay exactly the same. So the four triangles plus the small square always have the same total area. This is a dissection: cut a figure apart and move the pieces without stretching them. The logic test checks the actual cut pieces for every whole-degree shape from 30° to 90° and 600 fractional shapes: they always fill the square once.

The claim on the linked page

The applet's page points to Proof #10, which says: "The triangles in Proof #3 may be rearranged in yet another way that makes the Pythagorean identity obvious." Proof #3 computes c² = (a−b)² + 2ab; expanding gives c² = a² + b², the Pythagorean theorem. This is the second hinged variant: Hinged Pythagoras uses a different dissection of two squares into one (Proof #9), and Hinged Pythagoras 3 turns two triangles through a quarter turn (Proof #2). One quirk is kept from the original: its shape slider runs to 95°, but past 90° the cuts leave the square, so the pieces no longer tile it — the algebra still holds, the picture does not. Past about 269° the applet also fills the middle square and draws the dashed guide line, which this port keeps.

Set the shape to 45°: the small square shrinks to a point, and all four triangles fill the square. Then turn the hinge slider right around.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
